title: A request names a resource
body: The phone app asks for one order: `GET /orders/123`. In **REST**, the URL names a **resource**, here order 123, and the **HTTP method** says what to do with it: `GET` reads it. The API server reads the row from the database and answers with status **200 OK** and the order as **JSON**. This is the same trip as in SD 1: DNS, a connection, the server's work and the database.

title: An order with no address
body: The app sends `POST /orders` to place an order, but the delivery address is missing. The server checks the input and rejects it before touching the database, with **400 Bad Request** and a message saying which field is missing. This 400 tells the app the request itself must change: sending it again without an address will fail again. Not every 4xx works this way; after a 429, the same request may succeed once the rate limit resets. A 5xx code would say the server failed, which is not true here.

predict.question: The app sends POST /orders without a delivery address. Which status code should the server return?
options: 200 OK, with an error message in the body
predict.explanation: The caller sent an invalid request, so the answer is a 4xx code: 400 Bad Request. 200 would tell clients, caches and monitoring that it worked. 404 means the resource does not exist, but /orders does. 500 means the server failed, which would send engineers looking for a bug that is not there.

title: Scrolling down the history
body: The history comes in pages of 20 with an **offset**: page 2 is `OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20`, which skips the first 20 orders. While the customer reads page 1, three new orders arrive at the top of the list. Every older order moves down three places, so page 2 now starts with the last three orders of the old page 1: the customer sees them twice. A deleted order would make the next page skip one instead. Deep pages are also slow, because the database steps past every skipped row.

predict.question: A customer has seen the newest 20 orders on page 1. Three new orders arrive. The app then asks for page 2 with OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20. What does page 2 start with?
options: The order right after the last one shown
predict.explanation: The offset counts positions, not orders. The 3 new orders push everything down 3 places, so positions 21–23 now hold the last 3 orders of the old page 1, and they appear again. Nothing is skipped; a deletion would cause skipping instead.

title: Page with a cursor
body: A **cursor** names where the last page ended instead of counting positions: `?after=<cursor>`, where the cursor holds the time and id of the last order shown. The server asks for orders that come after that one in time-then-id order: `WHERE customer_id = 7 AND (created_at, id) < (<last time>, <last id>) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`. The id breaks ties between orders with the same time, so none is skipped. New orders at the top do not change what comes after the last one shown, so nothing repeats; they appear on refresh. With the index on `(customer_id, created_at, id)` from SD 4, each page reads a few index pages and 20 rows, however deep the customer scrolls.

title: Asking again and again
body: The live screen uses **polling**: every app asks `GET /orders/123` every 5 seconds. With 100,000 customers waiting at dinner time, that is 100,000 ÷ 5 = **20,000 requests per second**. A delivery takes about 30 minutes, so each app asks 360 times, but the status changes only about 6 times. About 98% of the answers say "no change".

predict.question: 100,000 phones each ask "any news?" every 5 seconds. How many requests per second reach the servers?
predict.explanation: Each phone sends one request every 5 seconds, so 100,000 phones send 100,000 ÷ 5 = 20,000 requests per second. 500,000 would be 100,000 × 5, which multiplies by the interval instead of dividing.

title: The server sends the news
body: With **server-sent events (SSE)**, each app opens one connection and keeps it open; the server sends an event only when the status changes. The 100,000 customers now cost 100,000 open connections and about 100,000 × 6 ÷ 1,800 s ≈ **333 events per second**, instead of 20,000 requests. SSE fits because the customer only listens. **WebSocket** keeps a connection open in both directions, which a chat with the driver would need. **Long polling** is a middle way: the server holds each request until something changes.

title: Two calls the order page needs
body: The team splits the program into **services**. The phone app calls the **API gateway**, which routes `/orders` to the Orders service. To build the order page, Orders needs the restaurant (40 ms) and the driver (30 ms). One after the other, the calls take 40 + 30 = 70 ms. They do not depend on each other, so Orders sends both at once and waits for the slower: about **40 ms**. Every call between services is another network trip that can be slow or fail.

predict.question: Orders needs the restaurant (40 ms) and the driver (30 ms), and neither call needs the other's answer. If Orders makes both calls at the same time, about how long until it has both answers?
predict.explanation: Calls made at the same time finish when the slower one does: 40 ms. 70 ms is the time when they run one after the other. 30 ms is only the faster call, and Orders still waits for the restaurant.

title: When one service is slow
body: Drivers becomes slow and answers after 2 seconds. Without a **timeout**, every order page waits 2 seconds, and requests pile up in Orders and the gateway too. With a timeout of 200 ms, Orders stops waiting and shows the order and the restaurant with "driver location unavailable". Chains also multiply failures: if a request needs 5 services in a row, each available 99.9% of the time, it works only about 0.999⁵ ≈ **99.5%** of the time.
